prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat electronic bands in twisted bilayer graphene at a magic angle and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states in moire flat bands

statement.case_for: After the full first-round exchange I keep the single-part prize for magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene. The criterion I would make explicit, as the chair asks, is: first, did nature deliver something that was not demanded of it, and second, is the claim secure and reproduced. B013 passes both. Bistritzer and MacDonald (2011) predicted flat bands at a specific angle from a quantitative continuum model, and the 2018 experiments found gate-tunable correlated insulators and superconductivity at that angle. Independent groups have reproduced the phases and extended them to twisted TMDs, fractional Chern states and moire excitons. The open pairing mechanism concerns follow-on physics, not the existence of the flat-band platform, and Mehlig and Eriksson both make this point well, so I treat it as a matter of citation wording and not of maturity. I have tested my own position against B061, which now has four supporters. I do not doubt that it is sound, but on the criterion of a new regime of nature versus a refinement of an established measurement tradition I still rank B013 first, and I recognise that this is a weighting of criteria and not a count.
statement.case_against: The credit set is the real weakness, and the round-1 exchange has not removed it. Yuan Cao and Valla Fatemi, who carried the 2018 experiments, are outside any three-name configuration, as are Dean, Young, Ashoori and the earlier twisted-bilayer theorists Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto. A three-person cap cannot repair this, and I think the citation should be drawn around the prediction and the observed phases so that it does not claim to honour everyone who contributed. A prize in a field only eight years old is also fresher than the clock or ion-trap candidates, and I accept that a committee that weights completeness of confirmation above novelty of regime could reasonably choose B061 instead.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B061 first and says the clock's maturity is clearer, since every 10^-18 claim has been checked in independent laboratories, while the pairing mechanism and correlated states in magic-angle graphene are unsettled and the B013 credit set is contested in a way the clock's is not.
responses.response: Your atomic-structure argument for the magic wavelength and blackbody shift is persuasive, and it answers the worry that the clock is merely engineering. I still separate maturity of the claim from maturity of the interpretation. What B013 would reward, the flat-band prediction and the observed correlated and superconducting phases, has been reproduced many times and does not depend on the pairing mechanism. On credit I concede the point: the omission of Cao and Fatemi is a real defect that the clock does not share. But I read it as a limit of the three-name cap, one that the citation can state openly, and not a reason to prefer the narrower result. You said you would not oppose B013 if the credit can be settled, and I take that as the true remaining disagreement.

responses.point: Kroll prefers a fully defensible, exactly measured clock result over a broader prize with a contentious credit set, and notes that the redefinition of the second is still pending.
responses.response: I take the standard of a claim that cannot be reinterpreted seriously, and I accept that Katori and Ye is a cleaner pair than anything in B013. But the chair's question is which criterion should decide. If cleanliness of attribution decides, B061 wins and I would not call that wrong. If the prize is meant to recognise a discovery nature supplied, I think B013 is stronger, because the clock extends a measurement we already knew how to make while the moire result opened a regime nobody had asked for. I also note that the claim to Katori and Ye is not free of dispute either, given Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow and the PTB, NIST and SYRTE groups, so attribution is a matter of degree and not a clean contrast.

responses.point: Mehlig moved to B013, treats the pairing mechanism as follow-on physics, opposes dropping Bistritzer, and says the citation should name the prediction and the observed phases and not claim to credit all the experiments.
responses.response: I agree with all three points and this is where I have landed on the credit question. A two-name MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero version would credit the continuum model to MacDonald alone, although Bistritzer is first author of the joint 2011 paper. I see no principled rule for removing him while keeping the other two. The rule I would propose is that credit follows the decisive prediction (Bistritzer and MacDonald) and the decisive experimental programme (Jarillo-Herrero), with the citation worded around the prediction and the phases so that it does not claim to adjudicate who else contributed. I cannot claim that this is a perfect rule, but it is a stateable one.

responses.point: Eriksson wants the omissions stated openly in the citation and regards a two-name MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero version as defensible, while keeping Bistritzer as a defensible fall-back in the three-name set.
responses.response: I agree that the omissions must be stated openly and not treated as an oversight. Where I stay on three names is the same reason Mehlig gives: the prediction is a joint paper led by Bistritzer, and cutting him in order to get a cleaner pair would sacrifice the very prediction-then-confirmation structure that makes the case. I would not call the two-name version indefensible, but I think it is the weaker of the two.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, moved to B061 for its smaller attribution problem and realised consequences, keeps B013 as the first alternative, and would favour the compact two-name B013 version if the committee wants condensed matter.
responses.response: I appreciate the clarity of your reasoning, and you rightly note that the interpretation of the correlated states is still moving. I would answer that the committee is not being asked to adopt an interpretation: the citation should cite the flat-band prediction and the observed phases, where the evidence is firm. On the two-name option I differ for the reason already given, that Bistritzer's role in the 2011 prediction is not the weakest link but the origin of the prediction. I also share your caution on B009, which is why I keep it only as a distant alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can accept a three-name credit that leaves out Cao, Fatemi, Dean and the earlier twisted-bilayer theorists, or would prefer the cleaner two-name B061 attribution.

Whether the unsettled superconducting mechanism is a timing reason to defer, or only a constraint on citation wording; I treat it as the latter but cannot exclude that colleagues weigh it more heavily.
How the committee weighs novelty of regime against completeness of confirmation when members apply different criteria; my own weighting is a judgement, not a measurement.
My knowledge of the experimental condensed-matter and precision-metrology literature is secondhand, so I rely on the supplied credit names and on colleagues' accounts of lattice-clock priority.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile. My research is in string theory, quantum gravity and cosmology at Uppsala, and my documented connections (David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet, the Uppsala theory group) do not link to any shortlisted candidate or credited name. I note the disclosures of Kroll (Hall-laboratory lineage), Olsson (B056), Johansson (B018) and Pearce (B009 field proximity); none concerns B013, and I see no need for recusal on my part.
